course: Daily Milk Sales: Dairy Herd System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
A business plan for a dairy herd is not a document for the bank; it is your daily roadmap. Without it, you are guessing how many cows to milk, how much feed to buy, and what price to charge. With it, you know exactly where you are going and how to get there. In Africa, where milk demand is growing fastâurban consumers want fresh, affordable milkâa clear plan separates profitable farms from those that collapse after one bad season.

Think of your plan as five stages: 1) Goal Setting, 2) Market Check, 3) Resource Audit, 4) Financial Projection, and 5) Action Calendar. Each stage builds on the last. For example, if your goal is to sell 50 litres per day, your market check tells you if 50 litres can be sold at a profit, your resource audit shows if you have enough cows and feed, your financial projection calculates costs and income, and your action calendar tells you when to buy a cow, plant fodder, or hire help.

Why does this matter? Because dairy farming has thin margins. A cow eats 15 kg of feed per day; if you don't plan, you might overspend on feed or underfeed and lose milk. A simple plan helps you avoid common traps: buying too many cows before securing a market, ignoring dry seasons, or pricing below cost. It also helps you get loans or grantsâmany African agricultural banks and NGOs require a basic plan before giving funds.

Start small. Even a one-page plan covering these five stages is better than none. Write it in your local language if that helps. Review it every month. Adjust as prices change. The goal is not perfection but direction. With a plan, you can turn a few cows into a steady daily income that pays school fees, feeds your family, and grows your herd.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To create a business plan for your dairy herd, you don't need a computer or expensive software. A notebook, a pen, and a simple calculator will do. But a few specific tools make the job easier and more accurate. First, get a record bookâany exercise book will workâwhere you will write daily milk yields, feed costs, and sales. Second, a calendar (wall or phone) to mark seasons, vaccination dates, and breeding schedules. Third, a measuring tape or scale to weigh feed and milk; guessing leads to losses.

For market research, you need a way to talk to people: a phone to call local hotels, shops, or neighbours who buy milk. If you have a smartphone, you can use free apps like Kobo Collect or even WhatsApp to record prices. But paper works fine. Also, collect price lists from feed suppliers and veterinary offices. Keep receipts for everythingâfeed, medicine, transport. These are your evidence for costs.

For financial projections, you need a simple table. Draw columns for income (milk sales, manure sales, calf sales) and expenses (feed, labour, vet, transport). Use a calculator to add and subtract. If you have access to a computer, a free spreadsheet like Google Sheets or Excel can help, but a hand-drawn table is just as good. Remember to include hidden costs: water, electricity for cooling, and your own time.

Finally, get a folder or plastic bag to keep all papers dry and safe. In many African farms, records get lost due to rain or careless storage. A simple waterproof folder costs little but saves your plan. And if you can, find a mentorâan experienced dairy farmer or extension officerâwho can review your plan and give feedback. Their advice is a free tool that can save you from costly mistakes.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Follow these five stages to build your dairy business plan. Stage 1: Set Your Goal. Decide how many litres you want to sell daily and by when. For example, 'Sell 30 litres per day within 12 months.' Write it down. Stage 2: Check the Market. Visit local markets, shops, hotels, and neighbours. Ask: How much milk do they buy daily? At what price? Who else supplies them? If you plan to sell 30 litres, make sure there is demand. Note peak seasons (e.g., Ramadan, school terms) when demand rises.

Stage 3: Audit Your Resources. List what you have: number of cows, land size, water source, feed storage, labour. Then list what you need: more cows, feed, a cooler, transport. For 30 litres per day, you need about 6 to 8 lactating cows (each gives 4-5 litres daily). If you have 3 cows, you need to buy more or wait for calves to grow. Calculate feed: each cow needs 15 kg of feed per day, so 8 cows need 120 kg daily. Can you grow or buy that?

Stage 4: Make Financial Projections. Estimate income: 30 litres x 50 KSh per litre = 1,500 KSh per day, or 45,000 KSh per month. Estimate expenses: feed (120 kg x 30 KSh = 3,600 KSh/day), labour (500 KSh/day), vet and transport (300 KSh/day). Total daily expenses = 4,400 KSh. That means you lose money! So adjust: find cheaper feed, increase price, or reduce costs. Maybe sell at 60 KSh per litre and grow your own fodder. Recalculate until income exceeds expenses.

Stage 5: Create an Action Calendar. Break your goal into monthly tasks. Month 1: Build a simple shed and buy feed. Month 2: Plant fodder (e.g., napier grass). Month 3: Buy 2 cows. Month 4: Start selling to neighbours. Month 6: Approach a hotel. Month 12: Reach 30 litres. Write these on your calendar. Review weekly. Adjust as needed. This step-by-step method turns a dream into a practical plan.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: No market research. Many farmers buy cows first, then look for buyers. Fix: Before buying any cow, talk to at least 10 potential buyers. Confirm they will buy at a price that covers your costs. If not, change your plan. Mistake 2: Underestimating feed costs. Feed is 60-70% of dairy expenses. Farmers often forget dry season when pasture is scarce. Fix: Plan for year-round feed. Grow fodder like napier, maize silage, or buy hay in bulk during harvest when prices are low. Budget for 15 kg per cow per day.

Mistake 3: Ignoring animal health. A sick cow gives less milk and costs money. Many plans omit vet costs. Fix: Include a monthly vet budget (e.g., 2,000 KSh per cow per year for deworming and vaccinations). Also, set aside emergency funds. Mistake 4: Overborrowing. Taking a large loan for many cows without a proven market leads to debt. Fix: Start small. Prove you can sell 10 litres profitably before expanding. Use savings or small grants first.

Mistake 5: Poor record keeping. Without records, you don't know if you are making a profit. Fix: Record daily milk yield, feed used, and sales. Use a notebook. At the end of each week, calculate your income and expenses. Mistake 6: Selling below cost. Some farmers sell cheap to beat competition, but then cannot cover feed. Fix: Calculate your cost per litre (total expenses Ã· litres sold). Never sell below that. If competition is fierce, add valueâsell yoghurt or cheese, or deliver to customers for a premium.

Mistake 7: No plan for dry season. Milk production drops when cows eat poor feed. Fix: Store silage or hay. Reduce herd size if you cannot feed all cows well. Mistake 8: Ignoring labour. Family labour is not freeâit has an opportunity cost. Fix: Include a fair wage for yourself and workers in your plan. If the plan only works with unpaid labour, it is not sustainable. Fix these mistakes early and your dairy business will be stronger.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety in dairy farming is not just about avoiding injury; it is about producing safe milk that customers trust. First, personal safety: Always wash your hands with soap before milking. Wear clean clothes and boots. Cows can kick, so approach calmly and use a milking stool. Keep children away from the milking area. When handling chemicals for cleaning or treating cows, wear gloves and a mask. Store chemicals away from feed and milk.

Milk safety: Use clean, food-grade containers. Stainless steel or aluminium cans are best. Never use plastic jerrycans that held chemicals. Strain milk through a clean cloth or filter to remove dirt. Cool milk quicklyâif you don't have a cooler, use a shaded area or a bucket of cold water. Sell milk within 4 hours of milking if not cooled. Bacteria grow fast in warm conditions. If you sell raw milk, inform customers to boil it before drinking.

Animal welfare: Happy, healthy cows give more milk. Provide clean water at all timesâa lactating cow drinks 60-100 litres per day. Give them shade and enough space. Avoid beating cows; it stresses them and reduces milk let-down. Follow a regular milking scheduleâtwice a day, 12 hours apart. Vaccinate against common diseases like foot-and-mouth and anthrax. Deworm every 3-4 months.

Business best practice: Keep accurate records. Separate business money from personal money. Pay yourself a salary. Reinvest profits into feed and herd improvement. Join a dairy cooperativeâthey often provide training, better prices, and cooling facilities. Finally, be honest with customers. If you promise 10 litres, deliver 10 litres. Trust builds repeat sales. Safety and best practice protect your health, your cows, and your reputationâthe foundation of a lasting dairy business.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now it is time to write your own five-stage business plan for your dairy herd. Follow these steps and use a notebook. Step 1: Set Your Goal. Write one sentence: 'I will sell ___ litres of milk per day by ___ (date).' For example, 'I will sell 20 litres per day by December 2025.' Step 2: Market Check. Visit three potential buyers: a neighbour, a shop, and a hotel. Ask: How much milk do you buy daily? What price? Would you buy from me? Write their answers. If you cannot find buyers for your target litres, reduce your goal or find new buyers.

Step 3: Resource Audit. List your cows: how many are lactating? How many litres does each give? List your land, water, feed, and labour. Then list what you need to reach your goal. For 20 litres, you need about 4-5 good cows. If you have 2, you need to buy 2-3 more or wait for calves. Calculate feed: 5 cows x 15 kg = 75 kg per day. Can you produce or buy that? Write your gaps.

Step 4: Financial Projection. Use these numbers: Income = litres x price. Expenses = feed + labour + vet + transport + water. For example, 20 litres x 50 KSh = 1,000 KSh per day. Feed: 75 kg x 25 KSh = 1,875 KSh. Labour: 300 KSh. Vet: 100 KSh. Transport: 100 KSh. Total expenses = 2,375 KSh. You are losing 1,375 KSh per day! So adjust: increase price to 70 KSh (income = 1,400 KSh), find cheaper feed (e.g., grow your own), or reduce cows. Recalculate until income is higher than expenses by at least 20%.

Step 5: Action Calendar. Write monthly tasks for the next 12 months. Month 1: Build shed, buy feed. Month 2: Plant napier grass. Month 3: Buy 1 cow. Month 4: Start selling to neighbours. Month 6: Approach hotel. Month 9: Add second cow. Month 12: Review and set new goal. Finally, show your plan to an experienced farmer or extension officer for feedback. Revise it. Keep it where you can see it daily. This exercise turns your dream into a practical, money-making plan.

quiz.q: What is the first stage of the five-stage business plan?
quiz.explanation: The first stage is Goal Setting, where you decide how many litres you want to sell and by when.

quiz.q: Why is a business plan important for a dairy herd?
options: A) It impresses the bank only
B) It helps you avoid guessing and make informed decisions
C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: A plan acts as a roadmap, helping you know how many cows to milk, feed to buy, and price to charge.

quiz.q: How many lactating cows are needed to produce 30 litres per day if each gives 4-5 litres?
quiz.explanation: 30 litres divided by 4-5 litres per cow equals 6-8 cows.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in dairy business planning?
options: B) Buying cows before securing a market
quiz.explanation: Many farmers buy cows first and then look for buyers, which can lead to losses.

quiz.q: What tool is recommended for keeping records?
quiz.explanation: A simple notebook and pen are sufficient for record keeping, though other tools can help.

quiz.q: What percentage of dairy expenses is typically feed?
quiz.explanation: Feed is the largest cost, often 60-70% of total dairy expenses.

quiz.q: What should you do if your financial projection shows a loss?
options: B) Adjust by increasing price, reducing costs, or reducing herd size
quiz.explanation: You must adjust your plan until income exceeds expenses, such as by finding cheaper feed or raising prices.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an action calendar?
options: B) To break your goal into monthly tasks
C) To record daily milk yield
quiz.explanation: An action calendar helps you plan when to buy cows, plant fodder, and start selling.

quiz.q: Why is market research important before starting?
options: A) To know your competitors only
B) To confirm demand and price for your milk
quiz.explanation: Market research ensures there are buyers willing to pay a price that covers your costs.

quiz.q: What is a hidden cost often forgotten in dairy plans?
options: C) Water and your own time
quiz.explanation: Water, electricity for cooling, and your own time are often overlooked but affect profitability.

quiz.q: What should you do with receipts for feed and medicine?
options: B) Keep them as evidence of costs
quiz.explanation: Receipts help you track expenses accurately and prove costs if needed for loans.

quiz.q: What is a good way to store your business plan papers?
options: C) Keep them in your pocket
D) Store in the cow shed
quiz.explanation: A waterproof folder protects records from rain and damage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended daily feed per lactating cow?
quiz.explanation: A lactating cow needs about 15 kg of feed per day for good milk production.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake regarding animal health in business plans?
quiz.explanation: Many plans forget to budget for veterinary care, which can lead to losses when cows get sick.

quiz.q: How can you avoid selling below cost?
options: A) Sell cheap to beat competition
B) Calculate your cost per litre and never sell below it
quiz.explanation: Knowing your cost per litre ensures you set a price that covers expenses and yields profit.

quiz.q: What is a best practice for milking hygiene?
options: B) Wash hands with soap before milking
D) Store milk in chemical jerrycans
quiz.explanation: Washing hands with soap prevents contamination and keeps milk safe.

quiz.q: Why should you cool milk quickly?
options: A) To make it taste better
quiz.explanation: Cooling slows bacterial growth, keeping milk safe and fresh for longer.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good animal welfare?
options: A) Beating cows to make them move
B) Providing clean water at all times
C) Keeping cows in dark sheds
quiz.explanation: Clean water is essential for cow health and milk production.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm dairy cows?
quiz.explanation: Regular deworming every 3-4 months keeps cows healthy and productive.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of joining a dairy cooperative?
options: B) Access to training and better prices
C) You don't need to keep records
D) You can sell below cost
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives often provide training, cooling facilities, and better market prices.

quiz.q: In the practical exercise, what is the first step?
quiz.explanation: The first step is to set a specific goal for daily milk sales and a deadline.

quiz.q: What should you do if your resource audit shows you have fewer cows than needed?
options: B) Buy more cows or wait for calves to grow
quiz.explanation: You can either buy additional cows or wait for existing calves to mature and start lactating.

quiz.q: What is a recommended way to handle dry season feed shortage?
options: C) Let cows graze on dry grass
quiz.explanation: Storing silage or hay during harvest ensures feed availability in dry seasons.

quiz.q: Why is it important to pay yourself a salary in the business plan?
options: B) To ensure the business is sustainable
quiz.explanation: If the plan only works with unpaid labour, it is not sustainable; your time has value.

quiz.q: What is a key safety practice when handling chemicals?
options: A) Wear gloves and a mask
quiz.explanation: Wearing gloves and a mask protects you from harmful chemicals.

quiz.q: What type of container is best for milk?
options: A) Plastic jerrycan that held chemicals
B) Stainless steel or aluminium can
quiz.explanation: Food-grade stainless steel or aluminium cans are easy to clean and do not contaminate milk.

quiz.q: What should you do if you sell raw milk?
options: A) Tell customers to boil it
quiz.explanation: Informing customers to boil raw milk helps prevent milk-borne diseases.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in record keeping?
quiz.explanation: Failing to record expenses leads to an inaccurate picture of profitability.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for maintaining customer trust?
options: B) Be honest and deliver the promised quantity
quiz.explanation: Honesty and reliability build repeat sales and a good reputation.

quiz.q: In the financial projection, what does income equal?
quiz.explanation: Income is calculated by multiplying the number of litres sold by the price per litre.
